{{for|the law of energetics|Lotka's principle}}
{{Short description|Application of Zipf's law to publications by field}}
[[File:Lotka_law_for_the_15_most_populated_categories_on_arXiv_(2023-07).svg|thumb|Lotka law for the 15 most populated categories on [[arXiv]] (2023-07). It is a log-log plot. The x-axis is the number of publications, and the y-axis is the number of authors with ''at least'' that many publications.]]
'''Lotka's law''',<ref name="Lotke">{{cite journal |last=Lotka |first=Alfred J. |date=1926 |title=The frequency distribution of scientific productivity |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24529203 |journal=Journal of the Washington Academy of Sciences |volume=16 |issue=12  |pages=317–324 |via=[[JSTOR]]}}</ref> named after [[Alfred J. Lotka]], is one of a variety of special applications of [[Zipf's law]].  It describes the frequency of publication by authors in any given field.<ref>{{cite book |last=Gupta |first=Jyoti |date=2015 |title=Citation Studies: A Performance Evaluation Technique of LIS Scientists |url=https://archive.org/details/citationstudiesp0000gupt/page/83/mode/1up |url-access=registration |location=New Delhi |publisher=Ess Ess Publications |isbn=978-8170007524 |pages=83–84 |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=De Bellis |first=Nicola |date=2009 |title=Bibliometrics and Citation Analysis: From the Science Citation Index to Cybermetrics |location=Lanham, MD |publisher=Scarecrow Press |isbn=978-0810867130 |pages=91–95}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Let <math>X</math> be the number of publications, <math>Y</math> be the number of authors with <math>X</math> publications, and <math>k</math> be a constant depending on the specific field. Lotka's law states that <math>Y \propto X^{-k}</math>.

In Lotka's original publication, he claimed <math>k=2</math>. Subsequent research showed that <math>k</math> varies depending on the discipline.

Equivalently, Lotka's law can be stated as <math>Y' \propto X^{-(k-1)}</math>, where <math>Y'</math> is the number of authors with ''at least'' <math>X</math> publications. Their equivalence can be proved by taking the [[derivative]].

[[File:Lotka plot.png|thumb|Graphical plot of the Lotka function described in the text, with C=1, n=2]]

== Example ==
Assume that n=2 in a discipline, then as the number of articles published increases, authors producing that many publications become less frequent. There are 1/4 as many authors publishing two articles within a specified time period as there are single-publication authors, 1/9 as many publishing three articles, 1/16 as many publishing four articles, etc.  

And if 100 authors wrote ''exactly'' one article each over a specific period in the discipline, then: 
{| class="wikitable"
! Portion of articles written
! Number of authors writing that number of articles
|-----
| 10 || 100/10<sup>2</sup> = 1
|-----
| 9 || 100/9<sup>2</sup> ≈ 1 (1.23)
|-----
| 8 || 100/8<sup>2</sup> ≈ 2 (1.56)
|-----
| 7 || 100/7<sup>2</sup> ≈ 2 (2.04)
|-----
| 6 || 100/6<sup>2</sup> ≈ 3 (2.77)
|-----
| 5 || 100/5<sup>2</sup> = 4
|-----
| 4 || 100/4<sup>2</sup> ≈ 6 (6.25)
|-----
| 3 || 100/3<sup>2</sup> ≈ 11 (11.111...)
|-----
| 2 || 100/2<sup>2</sup> = 25
|-----
| 1 || 100
|}

That would be a total of 294 articles and 155 writers, with an average of 1.9 articles for each writer.

==Other applications==

A generalized version of Lotka's Law has been used to model the number of [[Music recording certification|gold disks]] certified by the [[RIAA|Recording Industry Association of America]] from 1958 to 1989, and was found to be an almost perfect fit to the data.<ref name="Cox">{{cite journal |last1=Cox |first1=Raymond A. K. |last2=Felton |first2=James M. |last3=Chung |first3=Ken H. |name-list-style=amp |date=1995 |title=The Concentration of Commercial Success in Popular Music: An Analysis of the Distribution of Gold Records |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41810563 |url-access=registration |journal=[[Journal of Cultural Economics]] |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=333–340 |via=JSTOR}}</ref>

== Relationship to Riemann Zeta ==

Lotka's law may be described using the [[Zeta distribution]]:

<math display="block">f(x) =  \frac{1}{\zeta (s)} \cdot \frac{1}{x^s} </math>

for <math> x = 1, 2, 3, 4, \dots </math> and where

<math display="block"> \zeta (s) =  \sum_{x=1}^\infty  \frac{1}{x^s} </math>

is the [[Riemann zeta function]]. It is the limiting case of [[Zipfs law|Zipf's law]] where an individual's maximum number of publications is infinite.
